name: Strategic touching

lead: Strategic touching is the idea of using touch on purpose in social and dating settings to build connection. Examples include a handshake, a light touch on the arm or shoulder, or a high-five, used to come across as warm and comfortable.

Research on touch describes it as a channel of nonverbal communication that can convey emotions and strengthen bonds. The same literature stresses that its meaning depends on culture, gender, relationship and context, and that touch is not welcomed in every setting.

paras: In practice people use brief, socially normal touch such as handshakes or friendly contact with people they know, matched to the setting and the other person's responses. Practitioners emphasise watching the reaction and stopping when it is unreturned.
Unwanted touch can feel intrusive and damage trust or cause harm. Norms differ by culture and gender, and touch from a person with more power may be read as dominance.

chain: Builds connection and a friendlier impression
angle.text: Practitioners use touch to make interactions feel more connected. It affects how a person is perceived socially rather than their physical appearance.

lead: Strategic touching is a social-skills concept in which people use touch deliberately to build rapport and come across as warm and approachable. It belongs to the presentation side of looksmaxxing: how a person behaves alongside how they look.[1]

Touch is a form of nonverbal communication. Heslin's 1974 taxonomy sorted it into functional, social, friendship, love and sexual categories, and Hertenstein and colleagues in 2006 reported that touch alone can communicate distinct emotions such as gratitude, anger and fear.[1][2]
The meaning of touch depends heavily on intensity, location, culture and gender, so appropriate touch is context-bound, and consent matters.[1]

paras: Strategic touching applies research on social touch to everyday interaction. Wikipedia's article on haptic communication notes that touch meaning depends on intensity, duration, location and frequency, and that people in power touch subordinates more often, which can blur whether touch signals dominance or intimacy.[1]

Studies summarised on Wikipedia describe affective touch processing in the brain and in animals oxytocin release linked to stroking and grooming, though the human persuasion evidence is not described.[2] Whitcher and Fisher (1979) found a nurse's touch reduced anxiety in female patients but male patients reacted negatively, and cultures differ in how much touch is normal.[1] Martin (2012) found accidental touch from behind made shoppers leave sooner and rate brands more negatively.[1]
Because norms vary, touch can be unwelcome. Men are described as more likely to experience touch deprivation owing to prohibitions on same-sex touch.[1]
No studies found on strategic touching as a technique. Related research on social touch is summarised above.

timeline.event: Hertenstein et al. report touch can communicate distinct emotions.[1]
